LESSON 49 OF 106·Identity, Authentication and Access Control

Directory Services, SSO and Federation

Where entitlements really come from: directories as the source of truth, what single sign-on concentrates, and how a signed identity assertion crosses an organisation boundary.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

A directory service is the single place identities and their relationships are defined. Single sign-on and federation let one authenticated identity reach many systems, which is convenient and concentrates risk.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.

  1. Verification: Protect the directory as tier-zero infrastructure, with strong authentication and tight administrative access.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • The directory stores identities, their attributes and their group memberships.
  • Authentication is usually delegated to a single provider, and other systems accept its assertion of identity.
  • Federation extends that across organisational boundaries, so a partner identity can be accepted under agreed conditions.
  • Claims carry what the provider asserts, and trusting too much in a claim is how access leaks across boundaries.
  • Group membership decided in the directory becomes access everywhere, which makes the directory a high-value target.

The background

  • Directories existed to manage users and resources, and became identity stores once authentication moved into them.
  • Single sign-on was adopted to reduce password prompts, and the resulting dependency became a concentration of risk.
  • Federation protocols standardised cross-organisational trust, which also made misconfiguration more consequential.
  • Modern approaches increasingly use short-lived, audience-restricted tokens so a stolen assertion is limited.

Real-world examples

  • A directory compromise is worse than a single application compromise, because it affects everything that trusts it.
  • A group that includes both staff and service identities can grant a human the permissions intended for a program.
  • An application that accepts a token without checking the intended audience will accept tokens meant for another service.

What to look for

  • Check which systems trust the directory, since that is the blast radius of a directory compromise.
  • Check that tokens are audience-restricted, and that the receiving system verifies it.
  • Check group membership, since it is where most access is actually granted.
  • Check the lifetime of issued tokens and whether they can be revoked.

Key takeaways

  • Protect the directory as tier-zero infrastructure, with strong authentication and tight administrative access.
  • Restrict every application trust to the specific directory and services it needs.
  • Issue short-lived, audience-restricted tokens, and verify the audience on receipt.
  • Review group membership on a schedule, and remove identities that no longer need access.
  • Require multi-factor authentication on the directory itself, ahead of any other system.
